solution.concept_anchor: Rita — Varuna as its guardian deity
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because Indra is the most prominent deity in the Rigveda by number of hymns, and students may assume the most important deity is also the guardian of the cosmic moral order — failing to distinguish between Indra's war/rain function and Varuna's moral/cosmic function.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): Indra is the foremost Rigvedic deity by hymn count but is associated with war, storm, and rain — not cosmic moral order; Indra is not the guardian of Rita.
Eliminate option (c): Agni is the fire deity and the mediator between gods and humans through sacrifice — not the guardian of Rita.
Eliminate option (d): Rudra is associated with storms and is the precursor to Shiva — he is a fierce deity associated with disease and healing, not cosmic moral order.

Confirm option (a): Varuna (along with Mitra) is the guardian of Rita in the Rigveda — Varuna watches over truth and punishes falsehood; his role as moral deity makes him Rita's keeper → answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Indra-Varuna confusion is a classic UPSC Vedic literature trap. Indra's hymn count (largest in Rigveda) creates false primacy in students' minds. Varuna's moral authority is philosophically more significant but receives fewer hymns — this counter-intuitive relationship must be memorised explicitly.
solution.final_explanation:
Rita (cosmic moral order) is one of the most important theological concepts in Rigvedic religion. It governs both natural phenomena (the orderly movement of the sun, the seasons) and the moral sphere (truth, justice, right conduct).

• Option (a): Varuna — Correct. Varuna (along with Mitra) is the principal guardian of Rita in the Rigveda. He watches over human behaviour, records moral transgressions, and can grant forgiveness. His role makes him the closest Rigvedic deity to a moral sovereign.
• Option (b): Indra — Incorrect. Indra receives the most hymns in the Rigveda (~250 hymns) but is primarily a war deity (Vritra-slayer) and rain/storm god. He is celebrated for martial prowess, not moral oversight.
• Option (c): Agni — Incorrect. Agni is the fire deity and the divine intermediary who carries offerings to the gods; his role is sacrificial, not moral-cosmic.
• Option (d): Rudra — Incorrect. Rudra is the fierce deity of storms and disease in the Rigveda — the precursor to Shiva — with no role as Rita's guardian.

Value Addition:
• Varuna's importance declines sharply in the Later Vedic period as Indra and then Prajapati/Vishnu/Rudra become more prominent.
• The decline of Varuna is directly linked to the decline of Rita as the organising moral concept, replaced by Dharma.
• Varuna's role as surveyor of moral truth has been compared to the Zoroastrian deity Ahura Mazda — reflecting common Indo-Iranian religious heritage.

solution.concept_anchor: Agricultural hymns and economic shift in Atharvaveda
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because students who associate the Later Vedic period's economic changes with Brahmanas (which do describe complex rituals) may attribute agricultural content to Brahmanas rather than to the Atharvaveda.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a transition from pastoral to agricultural economy reflected in Vedic literature — identify which text documents this through agricultural hymns and folk content.
Eliminate option (a): Rigveda hymns reflect an early pastoral, tribal society — nature worship and cattle; agricultural economy is Later Vedic, not early Rigvedic.
Eliminate option (b): Brahmanas document elaborate sacrificial rituals and priestly consolidation — their content is ritual procedure, not agricultural folk hymns.
Eliminate option (d): Shatapatha Brahmana describes major Vedic sacrifices in detail — Ashvamedha, Agnichayana — not agricultural folk practices.

Confirm option (c): The Atharvaveda's content includes hymns related to agriculture, land, crops, and healing — reflecting the broader folk and economic life of the Later Vedic period, including the pastoral-to-agricultural transition → answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The key conceptual slip that option (b) exploits: students correctly identify Brahmanas as 'Later Vedic texts' and then incorrectly assume that all Later Vedic changes (including agricultural economy) are reflected in Brahmanas. The Brahmanas are Later Vedic but their content is strictly ritual — the economic and social dimensions of Later Vedic life are captured in the Atharvaveda's folk-oriented content.
solution.final_explanation:
The transition from a pastoral to an agricultural economy is one of the most significant social changes of the Later Vedic period (approximately 1000–600 BCE). This transition is reflected differently across Vedic texts.

• Option (a): Rigveda — Incorrect. The Rigveda reflects early Vedic pastoral society — rivers, cattle, tribal conflicts, and nature deities. Agricultural economy is not prominent in Rigvedic hymns.
• Option (b): Brahmanas — Incorrect. Brahmanas document the ritual procedures of the Later Vedic period — elaborate sacrifices and priestly authority — not agricultural folk practices or economic transitions.
• Option (c): Atharvaveda — Correct. The Atharvaveda's scope extends beyond ritual to include agricultural hymns (for fertile fields, good harvests, protection of crops), healing hymns, and domestic blessings. This breadth of content makes it a mirror of the evolving agricultural economy and broader folk religion of the Later Vedic period.
• Option (d): Shatapatha Brahmana — Incorrect. While it is the most important Brahmana text, its content focuses on sacrificial procedure (Ashvamedha, Agnichayana, Rajasuya) — not agricultural folk traditions.

Value Addition:
• The shift from pastoral to agricultural economy also explains the Atharvaveda's proto-medical content — settled agricultural communities developed more complex health management needs.
• The Atharvaveda's folk character makes it the most valuable Vedic text for the study of ancient Indian social history below the elite Brahmanical level.
• Later Vedic geography expanded eastward into the Gangetic plains — this eastward movement brought encounters with new agricultural landscapes reflected in Later Vedic literature.

solution.concept_anchor: Six Vedangas — correct enumeration
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d is deceptive because Jyotisha is a less commonly recalled Vedanga (often students can name four but forget Jyotisha and Chandas), making students wonder if it is real or fabricated — when in fact it is the genuine sixth Vedanga.
elimination_logic: Recall the six Vedangas: Shiksha, Kalpa, Vyakarana, Nirukta, Chandas, Jyotisha — these are the canonical six.
Check option (a): Shiksha (phonetics) — genuine Vedanga; belongs.
Check option (b): Itihasa (history/epic tradition) — this is NOT a Vedanga; it refers to the Mahabharata and Ramayana tradition and is part of Smriti literature, not a limb of the Veda.
Check option (c): Nirukta (etymology) — genuine Vedanga; belongs.
Check option (d): Jyotisha (astronomy/calendar) — genuine sixth Vedanga; belongs.
Option (b) — Itihasa — is the odd one out → answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Itihasa appears in the same breath as Vedic literature in many classroom discussions, especially when teachers contrast Shruti and Smriti. Students who hear 'Vedic corpus + Itihasa' repeatedly may subconsciously classify Itihasa as belonging to the Vedic auxiliary tradition. Only explicit memorisation of the six-Vedanga list prevents this plausible-fabrication error.
solution.final_explanation:
The six Vedangas are specific auxiliary disciplines necessary for the correct understanding, pronunciation, and ritual application of the Vedic texts. They are part of Smriti literature (human-composed) but are intimately associated with the Vedas.

• Option (a): Shiksha — genuine Vedanga (phonetics — correct pronunciation of Vedic mantras). Belongs.
• Option (b): Itihasa — NOT a Vedanga. Itihasa ('thus it was') refers to the epics — Mahabharata and Ramayana — and is a category of Smriti literature distinct from the Vedangas. This is the odd one out.
• Option (c): Nirukta — genuine Vedanga (etymology — Yaska's Nirukta is the foundational text). Belongs.
• Option (d): Jyotisha — genuine Vedanga (astronomy/calendrical science — used to fix auspicious times for Vedic rituals). Belongs.

Value Addition:
• The six Vedangas mnemonic: Shiksha (mouth of Veda), Vyakarana (grammar = face), Chandas (feet), Nirukta (ears), Jyotisha (eyes), Kalpa (hands) — this limb-metaphor appears in ancient texts.
• Itihasa, Purana, and Dharmashastra are all Smriti but are NOT Vedangas.
• The Vedangas evolved to preserve the Vedas accurately as the Sanskrit language changed over centuries — their development reflects anxieties about textual preservation.

solution.concept_anchor: Upanishadic Brahman-Atman — absent in early Rigveda

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: The concept of Brahman as the universal absolute reality and Atman as the individual self — and the philosophical inquiry into their relationship — are distinctly Upanishadic contributions, not present in early Rigvedic polytheistic hymns.
statement_analysis.reason: Early Rigvedic hymns are polytheistic and address natural deities (Indra, Agni, Varuna). The Brahman-Atman philosophical framework is an Upanishadic development — not present in the Samhita layer.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: The distinction between Saguna Brahman (Brahman with attributes) and Nirguna Brahman (Brahman without attributes) is first articulated in the Rigveda's Nasadiya Sukta, which represents the earliest Vedic approach to the concept of an ultimate impersonal reality.
statement_analysis.reason: The Saguna-Nirguna Brahman distinction is a later Vedantic philosophical debate — it is NOT articulated in the Nasadiya Sukta. The Nasadiya Sukta expresses cosmological skepticism but does not use the terminology of Saguna-Nirguna Brahman; this distinction developed within Upanishadic and post-Upanishadic Vedantic discourse.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because students who know the Nasadiya Sukta is philosophically significant may accept Statement 2's claim that it addresses the 'concept of an ultimate impersonal reality' — partially true in spirit but the specific Saguna-Nirguna distinction is a scope-extension beyond what the Nasadiya Sukta actually contains.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Brahman-Atman identity framework = Upanishadic, absent in early Rigvedic polytheism — well-established; Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Saguna-Nirguna Brahman distinction attributed to Nasadiya Sukta — the Nasadiya Sukta expresses cosmological wonder and skepticism but does NOT use the Saguna-Nirguna Brahman framework; that is a post-Upanishadic Vedantic vocabulary; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Reading later Vedantic vocabulary back into earlier texts is a classic sophistication-trap in UPSC Vedic literature questions. Students who correctly recall that Nasadiya Sukta is philosophical and that it engages with 'ultimate reality' may incorrectly accept the Saguna-Nirguna attribution. The specific vocabulary (Saguna, Nirguna) and the specific distinction (personal vs impersonal ultimate) belong to post-Upanishadic Vedanta — not to a Rigvedic hymn, however philosophically advanced.
solution.final_explanation:
The Brahman-Atman conceptual framework is one of the sharpest markers distinguishing Upanishadic thought from earlier Rigvedic religion.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Rigveda is characterised by polytheistic hymns addressed to natural deities — Indra, Agni, Varuna, Soma. The Brahman as universal absolute and Atman as individual self, and the inquiry into their identity or relationship, emerge only in the Upanishadic layer of literature. Projecting this concept back into the Rigveda would be anachronistic.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Nasadiya Sukta (RV 10.129) is philosophically remarkable for its skeptical inquiry into cosmic origins — it asks who, if anyone, knows the origin of creation, and whether even the creator knows. This is cosmological skepticism, not the Saguna-Nirguna Brahman distinction. The Saguna-Nirguna debate is a post-Upanishadic Vedantic philosophical development — terms and concepts of much later provenance than the Nasadiya Sukta.

Value Addition:
• Saguna Brahman (Brahman with qualities = personal God = Ishvara) is the focus of devotional Bhakti traditions; Nirguna Brahman (without attributes = pure consciousness) is central to Advaita Vedanta.
• The Nasadiya Sukta is often cited as evidence that ancient India had a tradition of philosophical skepticism and agnosticism — remarkable for a religious text.
• The Brahman-Atman framework presupposes a level of philosophical abstraction that requires the monistic intellectual environment of the Upanishadic period.

solution.concept_anchor: Women's status decline — Early to Later Vedic period
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because students who correctly identify A as true (women's status declined in the Later Vedic period) and R as true (Brahmanas consolidate priestly male authority) may assume R automatically explains A — without checking whether priestly consolidation is the specific cause of women's status decline.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — 'The status of women in Vedic society declined from the early Rigvedic period, when women like Lopamudra composed hymns and Gargi participated in philosophical debates, to the Later Vedic period' — Yes, this is factually correct and well-documented.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — 'The Later Vedic period witnessed the increasing complexity of sacrificial rituals and the consolidation of Brahmanical priestly authority, which was exclusively male in composition' — Yes, this is factually correct.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes, the rise of a male-dominated priestly class with exclusive ritual authority is precisely the social mechanism that marginalised women's participation in the intellectual and ritual life of Vedic society. R is a genuine causal explanation of A.
A correct + R correct + R explains A → correct option is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question deliberately makes the correct answer option (a) — both A and R correct with R explaining A — to test whether students can affirm a genuine causal relationship rather than defaulting to option (b) out of exam habit. Students over-trained on 'watch out for false causal links' may overcorrect and choose (b) here, missing the valid explanation. The assertion-reason format requires fresh evaluation of each pair, not a habitual response.
solution.final_explanation:
The comparison of women's status between the early Rigvedic and Later Vedic periods is an important social history question. The literary evidence supports both the decline and its cause.

• Assertion (A): Correct. The Rigveda contains evidence of female hymn-composers (Rishikas) like Lopamudra, Vishvavara, and Ghosa. Upanishadic texts like Brihadaranyaka show women like Gargi debating in royal courts. By the Later Vedic period and into the Dharmashastra period, women's access to Vedic education and ritual participation was sharply curtailed.
• Reason (R): Correct. The Later Vedic period's defining social feature was the consolidation of a hereditary, male-dominated Brahmanical priestly class whose authority derived from exclusive mastery of complex sacrificial procedures. This priestly monopoly systematically excluded women from ritual participation, which was the primary intellectual and social arena of the age.
• Causal relationship: R directly explains A. The exclusion of women from the male-dominated ritual complex is the primary mechanism of their intellectual and social marginalisation in the Later Vedic period.

Correct option: (a)

Value Addition:
• Lopamudra's Rigvedic hymns and Gargi's Upanishadic debates are often cited in discussions of gender equality in ancient India — they represent a pre-decline baseline.
• The Manusmriti (Dharmashastra tradition) marks the formal legal codification of women's subordination — a process that began in the Later Vedic period.
• Upanayana (sacred thread ceremony) was originally available to women — its exclusion in later periods is a marker of declining status.

Reason (R): The Later Vedic period witnessed the increasing complexity of Vedic sacrificial rituals and the consolidation of a hereditary, male-dominated Brahmanical priestly authority, which controlled access to ritual and learning.

(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

solution.concept_anchor: Correct characterisations of four Vedas

statement_analysis.statement: The Rigveda is considered the oldest of the four Vedas and serves as the primary source for the Samaveda's hymn content.
statement_analysis.reason: The Rigveda is universally regarded as the oldest Veda; the Samaveda draws most of its textual content from Rigvedic hymns, which are set to melody.

statement_analysis.statement: The Yajurveda is the only Veda that contains both prose and verse compositions, and its primary function was to provide ritual instructions for the Adhvaryu priest during sacrificial ceremonies.
statement_analysis.reason: The Yajurveda's prose-verse combination and its role as the Adhvaryu priest's manual for sacrificial action are both accurate and well-documented.

statement_analysis.statement: The Samaveda is a collection of original hymns celebrating the philosophical wisdom of the sages, distinct from and independent of the Rigvedic hymn tradition.
statement_analysis.reason: The Samaveda is largely derived from Rigvedic hymns set to melody — it is NOT a collection of original independent hymns. Its distinctiveness lies in its melodic arrangement (Saman = melody), not in original philosophical content.

statement_analysis.statement: The Atharvaveda, though last to achieve canonical recognition, is associated with the Brahman priest's supervisory role in sacrificial ceremonies.
statement_analysis.reason: The Atharvaveda is associated with the Brahman priest (the overall supervisor of the sacrifice), and its canonical recognition came later than the other three Vedas — both facts are correct.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d is deceptive because students who know Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct might not carefully examine Statement 3, especially if they loosely associate Samaveda with 'wisdom' traditions (Chandogya Upanishad belongs to Samaveda).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Rigveda as oldest + source for Samaveda — both correct; count 1.
Evaluate Statement 2: Yajurveda = prose and verse + Adhvaryu priest — both correct; count 2.
Evaluate Statement 3: Samaveda as 'original independent hymns' — incorrect; Samaveda is largely derived from Rigveda; Statement 3 fails; do not count.
Evaluate Statement 4: Atharvaveda + Brahman priest + late canonical recognition — both correct; count 3.
Three statements correct → answer is (c) — Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation of the Samaveda's associated Upanishadic tradition (Chandogya = major philosophical Upanishad) with the Samaveda Samhita's own content is the trap mechanism in Statement 3. Students who correctly recall 'Chandogya = Samaveda tradition' may extend this to conclude that the Samaveda Samhita itself is philosophically original — ignoring that the Samhita is a chanting manual built on borrowed Rigvedic hymns.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests precise knowledge of all four Vedas simultaneously, requiring students to evaluate one claim per Veda.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Rigveda's antiquity and its role as the source text for Samaveda's hymn content are both foundational facts.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Yajurveda's prose-verse composition and its use by the Adhvaryu priest are the defining textual and functional characteristics of this Veda.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Samaveda is NOT a collection of original hymns. Approximately 75 of its verses are original; the vast majority are Rigvedic hymns arranged with melodic notation (Saman). Calling it 'distinct from and independent of the Rigvedic hymn tradition' is false.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The Atharvaveda was initially excluded from the Trayi Vidya (three-Veda canon) and achieved full canonical recognition later. The Brahman priest's supervisory role using Atharvaveda is the standard four-priest assignment.

Three correct → Only three.

Value Addition:
• The Samaveda's philosophical importance comes through its associated Upanishads (Chandogya, Kena) — not through the Samhita text itself.
• Trayi Vidya (three-Veda canon) = Rigveda + Samaveda + Yajurveda — the original canonical trio before Atharvaveda's inclusion.
• The Brahman priest's use of the Atharvaveda explains why that Veda contains content related to averting ritual errors — a supervisory text needs knowledge of what can go wrong.

solution.concept_anchor: Katha Upanishad — Nachiketa-Yama dialogue
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad contains several dialogue-format passages (with King Janaka, Gargi, Maitreyi) that students may confuse with the Nachiketa-Yama framing, especially if they recall 'philosophical dialogue on death' but not the specific names.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): The Chandogya Upanishad's signature narrative is Uddalaka Aruni teaching Shvetaketu — Tat Tvam Asi and Panchagni Vidya — not the Nachiketa-Yama death dialogue.
Eliminate option (c): Brihadaranyaka Upanishad contains Yajnavalkya's debates with Janaka, Gargi, and Maitreyi — not the Nachiketa story.
Eliminate option (d): Mundaka Upanishad addresses Para-Apara Vidya and contains Satyameva Jayate — not the Nachiketa narrative.

Confirm option (a): The Katha Upanishad is the text in which the young Nachiketa travels to Yama's realm and, through persistent questioning, receives the teachings on the immortal Atman — answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Nachiketa-Yama entity-swap exploits the fact that Yama (death) as a philosophical interlocutor is uniquely memorable, but students may not fix this specific narrative to the Katha Upanishad rather than the larger, more frequently cited Brihadaranyaka or Chandogya Upanishads. Anchoring specific Upanishadic narratives to their specific texts is essential for exam precision.
solution.final_explanation:
The Katha Upanishad is celebrated for its framing narrative as much as its philosophical content. Young Nachiketa is sent to Yama (the god of death) by his father Vajashravasa. After waiting three days without hospitality, Yama offers Nachiketa three boons. Nachiketa chooses as his third boon the knowledge of what happens after death — leading to the Upanishad's central teaching on the immortal Atman.

• Option (a): Katha Upanishad — Correct. The Nachiketa-Yama narrative is the defining feature of this Upanishad, making it unique among principal Upanishads for its mythological frame.
• Option (b): Chandogya Upanishad — Incorrect. Contains Tat Tvam Asi, Panchagni Vidya, and the Uddalaka-Shvetaketu dialogues — not Nachiketa.
• Option (c): Brihadaranyaka Upanishad — Incorrect. Contains Yajnavalkya's debates on Atman with Janaka, Gargi, and Maitreyi — not the Nachiketa story.
• Option (d): Mundaka Upanishad — Incorrect. Contains Para-Apara Vidya distinction and Satyameva Jayate — not this narrative.

Value Addition:
• Katha Upanishad belongs to the Krishna Yajurveda tradition (Taittiriya recension).
• The Katha's phrase 'Uttishtata, jagrata, prapya varan nibodhata' (Arise, awake, seek the great and learn) was made famous by Swami Vivekananda.
• Among the 10 Dasopanishads, Katha is the most widely taught for its narrative accessibility alongside its philosophical depth.

solution.concept_anchor: Shruti vs Smriti — Vedangas as Smriti, Kalpa sub-divisions

statement_analysis.statement: The authority hierarchy in the Hindu textual tradition places Shruti above Smriti — meaning that in cases of conflict between revealed Vedic texts and human-composed texts such as Dharmashastra, the Vedic corpus takes precedence.
statement_analysis.reason: The Shruti-supersedes-Smriti hierarchy is a foundational principle of Hindu legal and philosophical tradition — Dharmashastra (Smriti) cannot override Vedic injunctions (Shruti).

statement_analysis.statement: The Kalpa Sutras, a subdivision of the Vedanga known as Kalpa, are classified as Shruti because they directly govern the performance of Vedic sacrifices and are therefore as authoritative as the Vedic Samhitas themselves.
statement_analysis.reason: Kalpa Sutras are Smriti (human-composed), not Shruti. Despite governing Vedic sacrifice, they are auxiliary compositions and do not share the revealed status of the Samhitas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas, and Upanishads.

statement_analysis.statement: The Grihya Sutras, forming part of the Kalpa Vedanga, deal with domestic rituals and life-cycle ceremonies (samskaras), while the Shrauta Sutras govern the major public Vedic sacrifices.
statement_analysis.reason: This correctly describes the subdivision of Kalpa: Shrauta Sutras = public Vedic sacrifice; Grihya Sutras = domestic rituals/samskaras; Dharma Sutras = legal-ethical conduct.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because students who correctly identify Statement 2 as the error (Kalpa Sutras are not Shruti) may mistakenly include Statement 1 as also wrong, reasoning that 'Shruti above Smriti' is too simple a claim for UPSC.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: Shruti supersedes Smriti in case of conflict — foundational Hindu legal principle; Statement 1 is CORRECT.
Check Statement 2: Kalpa Sutras classified as Shruti — this is wrong; Kalpa Sutras are Smriti; Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Check Statement 3: Grihya Sutras = domestic rituals; Shrauta Sutras = public sacrifices — correct subdivision description; Statement 3 is CORRECT.
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct → answer is (b) — 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Kalpa-Shruti conflation trap works through a guilt-by-association logic: 'Vedic sacrifice is Shruti-mandated; therefore the text governing Vedic sacrifice must be Shruti.' UPSC exploits this by making Statement 2's claim sound authoritative and logical. Students must remember: only the Samhita-Brahmana-Aranyaka-Upanishad sequence is Shruti; all auxiliary texts — however important — are Smriti.
solution.final_explanation:
The Shruti-Smriti classification is not merely academic — it determines textual authority in Hindu legal and ritual tradition. This question tests whether students can apply this classification correctly to auxiliary texts.

• Statement 1 — Correct: When Shruti (revealed) and Smriti (composed) texts conflict, Shruti prevails — this is a basic principle of Mimamsa and Dharmashastra interpretation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Kalpa Sutras govern Vedic sacrifice, but governing a sacred activity does not make a text sacred in the same way. Kalpa Sutras are Smriti — human compositions, however authoritative within their domain. Only the four-layer Vedic corpus (Samhita → Upanishad) is Shruti.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Kalpa Vedanga divides into: Shrauta Sutras (public Vedic sacrifice — Agnishtoma, Ashvamedha etc.), Grihya Sutras (domestic rituals — birth, marriage, death, upanayana), and Dharma Sutras (social and legal conduct).

Value Addition:
• Grihya Sutras are crucial sources for reconstructing daily life, marriage customs, and educational practices in ancient India.
• Dharma Sutras (Apastamba, Gautama, Baudhayana) are precursors to the later Dharmashastra texts like Manusmriti.
• The Shrauta Sutras' descriptions of Vedic altars contain mathematical knowledge (Pythagorean theorem precursors) recorded in the Sulba Sutras.

solution.concept_anchor: Purusha Sukta — Mandala 10 as later addition implying later Varna system
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because the description of Purusha Sukta as containing the Varna reference is factually correct — students who stop at confirming the Varna content will accept (b) without noticing that Mandala 7 is wrong (it should be Mandala 10).
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Rita as a concept in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad — incorrect; Rita is specific to Rigvedic theology and is not prominently featured in Upanishads where Brahman-Atman replaces it.
Eliminate option (b): Purusha Sukta in Mandala 7 — incorrect; Purusha Sukta is in Mandala 10 (RV 10.90); Mandala 7 is one of the older family books.

Eliminate option (d): Nasadiya Sukta as 'affirmation of divine creation by Prajapati' — incorrect; Nasadiya Sukta is an expression of philosophical skepticism and cosmological agnosticism — it explicitly questions who (if anyone) created the universe.
Confirm option (c): The Nasadiya Sukta in Mandala 10 expresses philosophical skepticism about cosmic origins — this is the accurately described pair → answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap in option (b) is subtle — it correctly identifies the Purusha Sukta's content (four Varnas) but switches the Mandala from 10 to 7. Students who verify content-accuracy without checking Mandala number will select (b). This exploits the common exam pattern of partially correct options where one element is right and one is wrong — students must check every element of each option, not just the most salient one.
solution.final_explanation:
Both Nasadiya Sukta and Purusha Sukta are among the most examined hymns in UPSC Vedic literature questions, and their precise Mandala locations and content characterisations must be known.

• Option (a): Rita as a concept from Brihadaranyaka Upanishad — Incorrect. Rita belongs to Rigvedic theology, maintained by Varuna and Mitra. It is not prominently featured in the Upanishads — the Upanishadic organising concept is Brahman, not Rita.
• Option (b): Purusha Sukta in Mandala 7 containing the earliest reference to four Varnas — Incorrect. The Purusha Sukta (RV 10.90) is in Mandala 10, not Mandala 7. The Varna content is correct, but the Mandala number is wrong.
• Option (c): Nasadiya Sukta in Mandala 10 expressing philosophical skepticism about the origins of existence — Correct. RV 10.129 is the Nasadiya Sukta, correctly located in Mandala 10, and its content is precisely cosmological skepticism — not a creation account or divine affirmation.
• Option (d): Nasadiya Sukta as an affirmation of Prajapati's role in creation — Incorrect. This reverses the Nasadiya Sukta's meaning; it expresses agnosticism about creation, ending with 'perhaps even He does not know.'

Value Addition:
• Mandala 10 contains hymns added in a later compositional phase — the philosophical and social content of Nasadiya and Purusha Sukta reflects later Vedic intellectual developments.
• Prajapati becomes the dominant creator deity in the Brahmana period — not in the Rigveda.
• The Nasadiya Sukta's agnostic closing verse is often cited as evidence of ancient India's intellectual openness.
